title: 2. Business Model, Segments & Real-World Customer Economics
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the Four Engines — What Cyient Actually Sells and Who Pays

epigraph.quote: Consolidated revenue hides a world of difference between a software engineer billing $45 an hour, a factory assembling cockpit avionics, and a fabless team shipping power-management silicon.
epigraph.author: Operating Economics Principle

summary: Cyient operates across four distinct reporting segments: Cyient DET (Digital, Engineering & Technology, ~74.5% of Q2 FY27 revenue), Cyient DLM (Design-Led Manufacturing, ~17.6%), Cyient Semiconductors (~8.3%), and Cyient Others (~0.4%). Within DET, revenue is organized into Transportation & Mobility, Networks & Infrastructure, Strategic Units, and newly integrated TAO Digital—each carrying markedly different margin, working-capital, and contract economics.

web_blocks.html: By Q2 FY27 (quarter ended September 30, 2026), Cyient's consolidated revenue reached ₹2,235 Cr (+25% YoY) across distinct operating engines [1][2]. Treating Cyient as a single monolithic IT/ER&D firm is a mistake. DET engineering services carry ~14% EBIT margins and minimal inventory [2]. By contrast, DLM electronics manufacturing carries ~10–11% EBITDA margins and 200–300+ days of component inventory [3]. Meanwhile, Cyient Semiconductors earns product-IP gross margins alongside heavy R&D capitalization [4].

DET remains the sole profit anchor (₹237 Cr EBIT in Q2 FY27), while DLM's record order book faces upfront investment margin drag and Semiconductors posted a -₹30 Cr Q2 EBIT loss due to product R&D.

web_blocks.html: 1. Cyient DET — Transportation & Mobility (Aerospace, Rail, Automotive): Cyient's flagship heritage unit serves commercial aircraft OEMs, aero-engine makers, and rolling-stock leaders. Real-world customer example: For Airbus, Cyient executes a multi-year cabin and cargo engineering services contract supporting next-generation "Connected Cabin" programs [5]. Airbus faces acute engineering bottlenecks when customizing cabin layouts, passenger connectivity wiring, and overhead stowage structures across airline-specific configurations. Cyient's dedicated aerospace teams deliver structural stress analysis, electrical harness routing, and digital mockups under multi-year managed work-package agreements priced on outcome milestones and blended offshore-onsite billing rates. Similarly, for Pratt & Whitney, Cyient provides aero-engine component repair validation and engineering productivity proposals, while for rail OEMs like Alstom it handles rolling-stock structural and electrical design [3][6].

2. Cyient DET — Networks & Infrastructure (Connectivity & Utilities): This unit traces directly to Cyient's 1991 GIS roots. It helps telecom carriers and power or gas utilities map physical networks. Real-world customer example: Tier-1 North American and European telecom carriers use Cyient for Fiber-to-the-Home (FTTH) and 5G rollouts [7]. Cyient feeds LiDAR street scans, permit records, and copper maps into GIS tools [7]. Instead of sending field staff to survey every pole, Cyient delivers permit-ready fiber routes [7]. Work is billed per mile or per home passed, which speeds up rollouts.

3. Cyient DET — Strategic Units & TAO Digital (Mining, Energy, Health & AI): Strategic Units serve heavy industry, including mining plants, clean energy, and medical devices. In Q2 FY27, Cyient added TAO Digital Solutions (~$9.6M in its first month, ~$80M annualized) [8]. TAO brings Santa Clara-based AI data work, cloud upgrades, and platform software [8]. Real-world customer example: Global auto and health-tech firms hire TAO to modernize old ERPs and connected-car data stacks [8]. TAO builds cloud data lakes and AI workflows, shifting DET from CAD drafting toward software product work [8].

4. Cyient DLM (Design-Led Manufacturing — 52.2% Subsidiary): Listed separately on Indian exchanges, Cyient DLM builds mission-critical electronics where failure is unacceptable. Real-world customer example: Cyient DLM holds a multi-year production contract with Boeing Global Services (BGS), alongside clients such as Honeywell, Thales, ABB, and Bharat Electronics (BEL) [9][10]. It manufactures AS9100- and NADCAP-certified PCBAs, complex cable harnesses, and full "box-build" cockpit, landing, and radar sub-assemblies [9][10]. Unlike consumer smartphone EMS, DLM runs low-volume, high-mix contracts where qualification takes 18–36 months. Its order book hit a record ₹2,813.7 Cr as of September 30, 2026 (1.6x book-to-bill, with Aerospace up 62% YoY), and on November 14, 2026 it signed an exploratory MoU with Miniratna defense PSU Hindustan Shipyard Limited (HSL) for indigenous maritime and naval defense electronics—though MoUs do not translate immediately into firm backlog and upfront sales-leadership investments have pressured near-term net margins [14][15].

5. Cyient Semiconductors (Custom ASICs & Kinetic Technologies ASSPs): Supercharged by the April 2026 Kinetic Technologies deal (82.9% stake), this unit pairs custom silicon design with proprietary power-management chips [11][12]. Real-world customer example: For AI data-center hyperscalers and automotive Tier-1s, Cyient Semiconductors delivers turnkey custom ASICs spanning architecture, RTL/physical design, wafer fab coordination, and packaged silicon supply, alongside Kinetic's AEC-Q100 automotive load switches (such as the KTS1642Q) and eFuses [12][13]. On November 18–19, 2026, global foundry GlobalFoundries approved a $10 million strategic CCPS equity investment at a $490 million pre-money ($510 million post-money) valuation to support custom ASIC expansion and long-term wafer-supply access [16][17]. However, investors must balance this strategic validation against near-term unit-economics friction: Cyient Semiconductors posted a -₹30 Cr EBIT loss in Q2 FY27 due to upfront product R&D, management cautioned on the Q2 call that tight foundry utilization and memory shortages/costs will likely soften near-term growth pace, breakeven remains targeted for FY28 (with 1–2 quarters of potential slippage), and the GlobalFoundries filing discloses no binding wafer-volume or pricing commitment [16][18].

web_blocks.title: Geographic & Client Concentration Reality
paragraphs: In FY26, Cyient DET derived 50.7% of revenue from North America, 27.7% from EMEA, and 21.5% from APAC.

Client concentration remains meaningful: in Q2 FY27 (excluding TAO Digital), the Top 5 clients accounted for 32.8% of DET revenue and the Top 10 accounted for 45.5%—making retention at anchor accounts like Pratt & Whitney and Airbus mission-critical.

book_paragraphs: To make sense of Cyient, you and I need to open the hood and look at the four very different businesses sitting inside one consolidated profit-and-loss statement. By the September 2026 quarter, Cyient generated ₹2,235 Cr of quarterly revenue, up 25% year-on-year. On the surface that looks like a clean acceleration. Underneath, however, three-quarters of the business is still engineering services (where organic constant-currency growth was a modest +0.4% year-on-year), roughly a sixth is specialized factory manufacturing, and nearly a tenth is now semiconductor design and chip sales.

Start with the core engine: Cyient DET, which generated ₹1,664 Cr in Q2 FY27 and ₹237 Cr of EBIT at a 14.2% margin, along with ₹214 Cr of free cash flow. Within DET, Transportation & Mobility is the crown jewel. Picture an airline ordering fifty new Airbus jets with custom Wi-Fi, galley layouts, and overhead bin configurations. Airbus cannot easily spare internal engineers for every airline variant, so Cyient's aerospace teams step in under multi-year "Connected Cabin" contracts to handle structural stress analysis, electrical harness routing, and digital mockups. The same deep integration holds at Pratt & Whitney for jet engine component validation and at Alstom for rail rolling stock.

The second DET pillar, Networks & Infrastructure, is the direct descendant of Cyient's 1991 GIS mapping business. When a major North American or European telecom carrier rolls out fiber-optic broadband across thousands of neighborhoods, field crews cannot dig until they have permit-ready engineering blueprints. Cyient's spatial engineers take raw LiDAR street scans and municipal maps and convert them into digital fiber-routing designs, often priced per mile or per household passed. Alongside that, the newly acquired TAO Digital—which added $9.6 million in just its first consolidated month in Q2 FY27 and runs near an $80 million annual pace—brings Santa Clara-based cloud and AI data engineering for automotive and healthcare enterprises.

Now contrast that asset-light services world with Cyient DLM, which posted ₹393.1 Cr in Q2 FY27 revenue, up 26.5% year-on-year. Walk onto a Cyient DLM floor and you are not looking at software desks; you are looking at AS9100- and NADCAP-certified clean-room assembly lines building flight-critical circuit boards, cable harnesses, and complete cockpit or radar box-builds for Boeing Global Services, Honeywell, Thales, ABB, and Bharat Electronics. Because aerospace and defense electronics require years of qualification, DLM enjoys sticky multi-year order books—hitting a record ₹2,813.7 Cr in Q2 FY27 at 1.6x book-to-bill, reinforced by a November 14, 2026 maritime defense electronics MoU with Hindustan Shipyard Limited—but it earns 10–11% EBITDA margins, faces near-term margin pressure from upfront sales investments and memory-component tightness, and ties up heavy inventory.

Finally, look at the fastest-growing and most experimental engine: Cyient Semiconductors, which jumped 240.8% year-on-year to ₹184.7 Cr in Q2 FY27 following the $85 million majority acquisition of Kinetic Technologies and attracted a $10 million strategic CCPS investment from GlobalFoundries on November 18–19, 2026 at a $510 million post-money valuation. Here Cyient designs turnkey custom ASICs for industrial and automotive customers while selling Kinetic's catalog power-management chips—such as AEC-Q100 automotive load switches and eFuses, plus next-generation 800V+ power delivery solutions for AI data centers. Yet do not mistake top-line velocity for immediate profit: the segment absorbed a -₹30 Cr EBIT loss in Q2 FY27 due to product R&D, management flagged tight foundry capacity and memory shortages that may soften near-term growth, breakeven is pushed out to FY28 (with possible 1–2 quarter slippage), and GlobalFoundries' equity stake comes without a disclosed binding wafer-volume contract.

Why does this four-engine map matter so much for you? Because each engine demands different working capital, different management talent, and different capital intensity. DET generates cash with 66 debtor days and almost zero inventory; DLM ties up cash in 300 days of aerospace components; Semiconductors is burning -₹30 Cr per quarter in R&D while awaiting FY28 breakeven. And with Cyient's Top 5 DET clients still representing 32.8% of DET revenue and Top 10 representing 45.5%, the core services engine has to stay healthy to fund both the working capital of DLM and the R&D appetite of Semiconductors.

book_callouts.title: Services vs. Manufacturing vs. Silicon
book_callouts.text: Ask yourself: can one management team simultaneously optimize billable utilization in Hyderabad, factory-floor yield in Mysuru and North America, and fabless analog chip roadmaps in Silicon Valley? The strategic upside is real, but so is the operational complexity.

book_subsections.title: Why Customer Examples Reveal Switching Costs
paragraphs: When you trace real contracts—like Cyient DLM building aerospace assemblies for Boeing, DET engineers designing Airbus Connected Cabins, or Cyient Semiconductors qualifying ISO 26262 automotive silicon—you see why Cyient's customer relationships last decades. Switching an AS9100 aerospace supplier or re-qualifying an automotive power-management IC is slow and risky for the OEM.

At the same time, high switching costs do not immunize Cyient from volume pauses. When aerospace or telecom clients defer discretionary R&D budgets, as happened in FY25, DET's organic revenue stalls quickly—proving that sticky relationships protect against customer churn, not against client capex cycles.

Similarly, geographic concentration in North America (50.7% of FY26 DET revenue) and EMEA (27.7%) means Cyient's growth cadence is tied directly to Western industrial, defense, and telecom spending cycles.
